18.notes: Hint 3 lets the student answer without thinking, failing the hint-3 test in the standard. It reads: "Which option describes a patient following exactly what the doctor ordered?" By the point hints 1 and 2 have ruled out C and D as abuse, only A and B remain, and this hint is just a paraphrase of option A's own wording ("right dosage of prescribed drugs" becomes "exactly what the doctor ordered"; "patient" signals the medical-use option). A student can match the wording straight to A without reasoning about what drug abuse means, since B (trafficking) plainly has nothing to do with a patient at all.
18.fix: Two options are left. One is a patient taking medicine correctly, and one is a crime of dealing in drugs across borders. Which one is not wrongdoing?

24.notes: The solution's list of syllabus skill types is wrong. It states: "The WASSCE syllabus names the types of youth empowerment skills as manipulative, intellectual, communicative, creative or artistic, leadership, life-coping and value skills." The subtopic's own definition (youth-empowerment.skills) gives the syllabus list as life-coping, manipulative, intellectual, communicative, artistic, leadership, vocational and ICT skills. The solution silently drops vocational skills and ICT skills, the two skill types most directly tied to youth self-employment and modern work, and substitutes an invented category, "value skills", that is not part of this subtopic's list at all. A student memorising this list from the solution would learn the wrong syllabus content.
24.fix: The WASSCE syllabus names the types of youth empowerment skills as manipulative, intellectual, communicative, artistic, leadership, life-coping, vocational and ICT skills.

25.notes: In "Why not the others", the reason given for C states an unscoped absolute: "C. Self-reliance skills: these are on the list, because being able to support oneself is the main aim of youth empowerment." Youth empowerment has several aims (leadership, national development, employment, civic participation, etc.); calling self-reliance "the main aim" overstates a single aim as the definitive one, which a student would carry forward as fact.
25.fix: C. Self-reliance skills: these are on the list, because supporting oneself is one of the key aims of youth empowerment.

28.notes: The "How to tell" line states an unscoped absolute as a general fact about any country: "How to tell: a country can have only one army protecting its borders." This is not literally true of countries in general (some federations maintain state-level defence forces, e.g. the US National Guard); the claim needs to be scoped to Nigeria's federal system, where only the federal government keeps an army.
28.fix: How to tell: in Nigeria's federal system, only the federal government keeps an army to defend the whole country. States cannot keep their own armies, so defence is exclusive to the federal government.

35.notes: Hint 3 fully solves the question instead of narrowing to a genuine final choice. After hint2 eliminates pair A (it contains I, political apathy, a problem), three pairs remain: B, C, D. Hint3 reads: "Now make the same check for human trafficking and HIV/AIDS. You are looking for the pair in which both items are things a society cannot do without." This instructs the student to eliminate both B (contains IV, HIV/AIDS) and C (contains III, human trafficking) in one step, which leaves only D. Nothing is left for the student to decide: mechanically applying the hint's own rule produces the answer, so hint3 lets the student answer without thinking. The standard requires hint3 to narrow to two options and still leave the choice to the student.
35.fix: Now check pair B: HIV/AIDS (IV) is also a problem, so B is out too. That leaves two pairs, C and D. Look at each remaining item, III, VI, II and VII: is it something society needs, or a problem it is better off without? Which of the two pairs left is made up of two things society cannot do without?
